metadata.title: Knowledge-base d question answering by tree-to-sequence learning
metadata.abstract_summary: This paper proposes a tree-to-sequence learning approach to answer natural language questions using a knowledge base. The method models a query's structure as a tree and encodes the orders of entities and relations to better distinguish candidate queries.

sections.heading: Sen
sections.text: Su ∗ State Key Laboratory of Networking and Switching Technology, Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications, Beijing, China a r t i c l e i n f o Article history: Received 16 September 2018 Revised 8 August 2019 Accepted 8 September 2019 Available online 13 September 2019 Communicated by Dr Jie Wang Keywords: Question answering Knowledge base Neural network Tree to sequence a b s t r a c t In recent years, many knowledge bases have been constructed or populated. These knowledge bases link real-world entities by their relationships on a large scale, serving as good resources to answer factoid questions. To answer a natural language question using a knowledge base, the main task is mapping it to a structured query of the same meaning, whose results from the knowledge base will be used as the question’s answers. This mapping task is non-trivial since different questions can express a same meaning and many queries can arise from a knowledge base. To fulfill the task, an important thing is to model a query’s structure as it conveys a part of the meaning and affects word orders in the question. However, state-of-the-art methods based on deep learning have neglected query structures and focused only on capturing semantic correlations between a question and a simple relation chain. In this paper, we instead take a query as a tree, and encode the orders of entities and relations into its representations to better distinguish candidate queries of a given question. Overall, we first construct candidate queries of a given question from its linked entities, types and number operations. Then, we adopt an encoder-decoder framework which encodes a candidate query and decodes it into the given question, where the decoding probability is used to select the best query from candidates. During encoding, we propose a tree-based LSTM to properly model contexts of an entity or relation in a query, and one such tree-based LSTM runs from all leafs to the root while another runs reversely. During decoding, we propose to mix a generating mode and a referring mode to capture different levels of correlations between queries and questions. Experiments on two popular datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of both the tree-based encoder and the mixed-mode decoder. © 2019 Published by Elsevier B.V. 1.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.text: The rapid development of knowledge bases (KBs) including open-domain ones like Freebase [1] , DBPedia [2] and domain- specific ones like Thomson Reuters Knowledge Graph 1 has at- tracted much attention from different societies. To put those KBs into actual usage, a promising direction is to use them for an- swering factoid questions, as a KB can contain a huge amount of real-world facts for answering different questions, e.g., Freebase contains 2.4 billion facts, and it gathers knowledge for an entity which benefits answering complex questions about such entities, as shown in Fig. 1 (a). A KB is typically stored following the Resource Description Framework 2 (RDF) standard and can be queried using the SPARQL ∗ Corresponding author. E-mail addresses: zsg1990ok@bupt.edu.cn (S. Zhu), chengxiang@bupt.edu.cn (X. Cheng), susen@bupt.edu.cn (S. Su). 1 https://developers.refinitiv.com/tr-knowledge-graph . 2 https://www.w3.org/RDF/ . Protocol and RDF Query Language 3 (SPARQL) language. Hence, an- swering a question over a knowledge base can be resolved by map- ping it to a SPARQL query with the same meaning and return- ing the query’s results. Fig. 1 illustrates the facts related to Natalie Portman from Freebase in RDF, and the query expressing the ques- tion “What character did Natalie Portman play in Star Wars?” in SPARQL. Fig. 2 takes a further step by viewing entities as nodes, relations as links, a knowledge base as a graph and a query as a subgraph. From both figures, we can observe that a query is struc- tured in that it organizes certain entities and relations in a specific order. This structural information directly affects the meaning and should be modeled for a query to better distinguish possible inter- pretations of a question and enhance a QA model. Early methods for question answering over knowledge bases are mostly based on templates. Those methods manually label or automatically learn mappings from question syntax trees to query templates, where structures are modeled. However, templates only cover a small number of structures and lack the ability 3 https://www.w3.org/TR/rdf-sparql-query/ . https://doi.org/10.1016/j.neucom.2019.09.003 0925-2312/© 2019 Published by Elsevier B.V. Red nodes and links indicate the query from Fig. 1 (c). m.0k3qy8 is a CVT, a special kind of node in Freebase that combines more than two entities to form a fact. to generalize. Recent methods are mainly based on machine learning. They generate candidate queries by rules, and extract heuristically designed features from both the question and queries for ranking them. However, such features are relatively simple and cannot characterize structures well. Currently, methods have widely adopted deep learning. Those methods first determine a topic entity, then match its linked relation chains of one or two hops against the question with a neural network (NN), and finally add constraints to the matched chain. However, they use relation chains instead of full queries during matching, therefore barely utilize the structures. In this paper, we propose to encode the structure of a candi- date query into its representations to enhance its matching against a given question. Overall, our method first conducts entity, type and number operation linking of a given question and constructs candidate queries from these linked constraints, then matches each candidate query against the question. During matching, an encoder-decoder framework is adopted to encode a candidate query and decode it into the given question, where the probabil- ities of the question decoded from different queries are used for selecting the best one out of them. sections.heading: Related
sections.text: work In this section, we first review existing work on KB-QA, then introduce the attention-based sequence-to-sequence (seq2seq) model and explain its limitations if directly applied to this task. 2.1. Existing work on KB-QA Early methods for KB-QA are usually based on templates. Unger et al. [5] combines a hand-crafted lexicon and a set of rules to map a question into a query template, where common expres- sions are mapped into the structure while uncommon expressions are mapped into entity/relation slots for further disambiguation. Zheng et al. [6] generates question-query templates through align- ing a question corpus and a query workload. The alignments are achieved by representing a question as a graph following [7] , and calculating its edit distance to a query’s graph to find the matched query. Abujabal et al. [8] automatically generates templates using only Q&A pairs. Given a question with gold answer(s), it generates a query containing all the linked entities and achieves the highest F1 on the answer(s), and generalizes this query along with the de- pendency tree of the question into a template by replacing words, entities and relations with variables. All these methods consider the query’s structure corresponding to a question. However, they have limited templates which covers only a small portion of ques- tions, and are difficult to adapt to questions uncovered by their templates. Our method can handle questions even if their corre- sponding query structures are not observed during training. 66 S. Zhu, X. Cheng and S. Su / Neurocomputing 372 (2020) 64–72 Some methods adopt grammars like combinatory categorial grammar (CCG) to translate questions into queries. Kwiatkowski et al. [9] uses a probabilistic CCG to build a linguistically mo- tivated semantic logical form. The translation to a KB-specific query is performed by a learned ontology matching model. Reddy et al. [10] converts sentences to ungrounded graphs following CCG grammar and grounds it to Freebase using a feature-based model trained by surrogate graph pairs created from sentence denota- tions. These methods deal with a broader domain of questions, but are not robust to ungrammatical questions. Our method per- forms the matching procedure by deep learning, which will extract meanings of questions even if they are grammarly incorrect. Recently, methods based on machine learning becomes popu- lar. Berant et al. [11] over-generates candidate queries for a ques- tion through lexical mappings and rules, and extracts features from both the question-query pairs to rank the candidates, where the ranking model is trained using Q&A pairs. Berant and Liang [12] also over-generates candidate queries with rules, but trans- forms those queries into formal questions with another set of rules, and matches them against the original question using a feature-based model trained by a large question paraphrase cor- pus. Bao et al. [13] generates a set of triples for each span of the question text, and recursively combines these triples into a query to prune the searching space. Features over question-query-answer tuples are extracted to rank the queries and their answers for a question. Nevertheless, those methods adopt simple features to de- scribe both queries and questions, which is insufficient to capture a query’s structure or a question’s semantic. Instead, we explicitly capture a query’s structure and use embeddings for better captur- ing semantics. Deep learning and embedding techniques are developing rapidly and have been applied to the KB-QA task. Yih et al. [14] as- sumes that a query consists of a topic entity, a relation path of one or two hops and several direct constraints on the path. It focuses on improving accuracy of relation detection with a letter tri-gram CNN which captures deeper semantics. Following this assumption, Xu et al. sections.heading: Our
sections.text: method The framework of our method is illustrated in Fig. 3 . As shown in this figure, first, we conduct constraint linking to link each ques- tion mention to its possibly referring entities, types and number operations in the KB. Second, we use these constraints to construct candidate queries for the given question. Third, we encode each candidate query into a set of hidden states. Fourth, we decode each set of hidden states into the given question and use the decoding probabilities to select the best query. Fifth, we use the best query to query the KB and return answers. Now, we illustrate each part in detail. 3.1. Constraint linking To construct candidate queries for a question, the first step is to locate information in the KB which is possibly referred by the question, therefore constrain the construction of queries. Here, we consider three kinds of information, i.e., entities, types and num- bers. One such constraint can be mentioned by the question with a word or phrase, and we need to identify all the mentions then link them to the KB. For entities, we adopt the state-of-the-art entity linking tool S-MART [31] . It first recognizes mentions in the ques- tion, then assigns one or several entities to each mention over a confidence score. For types, we query all distinct types in Freebase, and link a type to the question if a question word or phrase ap- pears in it. For numbers, we adopt regular expressions and a pre- defined lexicon to detect (1) single numbers, (2) patters of com- parative words + a number like before 1978 , (3) superlative words like youngest , and map them to operations which might be later attached to a query. 3.2. Candidate query construction Once we link the question to entities, types and number oper- ations, we are ready to construct candidate queries. To accomplish that, our idea is to first build a graph by taking one entity from each mention as leaf nodes and linking them with intermediate nodes, then select an intermediate node as the answer, finally at- tach types and number operations to any compatible intermediate or answer node. Next, we illustrate this process step by step. Step 1: Growing intermediate nodes. First, we select one entity from each mention’s linked entities, e.g., Natalie Portman and Star Wars: Episode I - The Phantom Menace for “Na- talie Portman” and “Star Wars” in the running example question. They are leaf nodes. Then, we query all entities within one hop of each selected entity. i.e., Aleph Portman- Millepied and some other entities for Natalie Portman while George Lucas and others for Star Wars: Episode I - The Phan- tom Menace . Those are intermediate nodes grown from each leaf node. Step 2: Linking intermediate nodes into a graph. We search over combinations of intermediate nodes one from each leaf node. Whenever they are interconnected through no extra intermediate nodes, we recover their connections to leaf nodes and keep the whole graph. Sometimes, intermedi- ate nodes from different leaf nodes can be the same, we directly take them as connected. For example, m.0k3qy8 is grown from both Natalie Portman and Star Wars: Episode I - The Phantom Menace , thus we build a graph Natalie Port- man film −−→ m.0k3qy8 starring ←−−−− Star Wars: Episode I - The Phan- tom Menace . Step 3: Selecting an intermediate node as the answer. We select an intermediate node in an above graph as the answer vari- able, and make the other intermediate nodes regular vari- ables. If the selected node is a CVT in Freebase, we ex- tend one hop and take the further node as the answer variable. Following the above example, m .0 k 3 qy 8 is a CVT and we extend character −−−−−→ Padmé Amidala to it, then convert m .0 k 3 qy 8 to a regular variable and Padmé Amidala to the answer variable. Step 4: Attaching types and number operations. sections.heading: Experiment
sections.text: 4.1. Datasets The adopted datasets are WebQuestions [11] and WebQues- tionsSP [34] . WebQuestions contains 3778 questions for training and 2032 for testing, where each question is paired with gold answers. WebQuestionsSP removes questions from WebQuestions whose meaning cannot be expressed by a query of the knowl- edge base, and label each remaining question with a gold SPARQL query, resulting in 3098 questions for training and 1639 for testing. The questions vary from about a single subject-relation pair to in- volving four relations and aggregations. The underlying knowledge base for both datasets is the last available Freebase dump released in 2015-08-09, and we remove relations belonging to the common or base domain since they are not about world knowledge. 4.2. Evaluation metrics In the test set, any question q has a gold answer set o ∗ of one or several answers. Given q , our method produces a query a which returns an answer set o . Therefore, precision, recall and F1 should be calculated for each test question: P rec ( q ) = | o ∩ o ∗ | | o | , Rec ( q ) = | o ∩ o ∗ | | o ∗ | , F 1 = 2 P rec ( q ) ∗ Rec ( q ) P rec ( q ) + Rec ( q ) . (13) Then, the evaluation metric would be the F1 averaged over all test questions. 4.3. Model and training details We use pre-trained word embeddings Glove [35] with 300 di- mension to prepare embeddings for entities, types, number opera- tions and relations. For relation embeddings, notice that a relation in Freebase is actually in the form of /domain/type/property , where each part contains several words. We remove the first two parts and average word embeddings in the third part to represent a re- lation. For types, we follow a similar procedure and only average embeddings of the last part. For entities and number operations, we average all their word embeddings. These embeddings are then transformed into 128 dimension by different matrices. The hidden size of LSTMs in the tree-based encoder and mixed- mode decoder is also 128. Word embeddings are fixed during training while transformation matrices and LSTMs will be adjusted. Those parameters are uniformly initialized in [-0.08, 0.08]. We use RMSProp to train our model which is a back propagation algorithm that automatically adapts learning rate. Minibatch is adopted with a size of 30, and the margin λ is 10. For questions with more than 30 negative samples in the training set, we randomly select 30 negative samples. Notice that WebQuestions gives gold answers instead of queries as supervision, we therefore find the one among candidates achieving the highest F1 as a surrogate gold query to train our model. sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.text: In this paper, we propose a method for question answering over a knowledge base. It first constructs candidate queries for a ques- tion from its linked entities, then matches each query against the question with a neural network based model. The matching model encodes a query into a set of hidden states and decodes them into the question, where the decoding probability is used to select the best query. The encoder takes a query as a tree, and summarizes a node or link’s tree-based contexts into its hidden state, there- fore encoding the whole query’s structure. The decoder has two modes which respectively give a probability to the current word of the question, and uses a gate to combine the two probabili- ties according to the previous words. The generating mode focuses on semantic-level correlations, and the referring mode focuses on surface-level correlations as well as language variations uncovered by the training data. Experiments on two popular KB-QA datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of proposals in our method.
